title: CTS Parables of the Bible — Unit 13: The Vineyard and the Tenants

blocks.en: 🍇 Parables of the Bible — Unit 13: The Vineyard and the Tenants
blocks.es_reference: 🍇 Las Parábolas de la Biblia — Unidad 13: La Viña y los Labradores

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone." — Matthew 21:42 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "La piedra que desecharon los edificadores, ha venido a ser cabeza del ángulo." — Mateo 21:42 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation
blocks.es_reference: Orientación

blocks.en: In Unit 2 we heard Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard: God planted Israel like a choice vine, cared for it, and looked for good grapes, but it produced wild grapes. Now, some seven centuries later, Jesus stands in the temple courts in Jerusalem and begins a story that every listener recognizes at once: "There was a certain landowner who planted a vineyard and set a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it and built a tower" (Matthew 21:33). The hedge, the winepress, and the tower come straight from Isaiah 5. The crowd knows this song. But Jesus adds something Isaiah never said. This time the problem is not the vineyard. It is the tenants.
blocks.es_reference: En la Unidad 2 oímos el Canto de la Viña de Isaías: Dios plantó a Israel como una vid escogida, la cuidó y esperó buenas uvas, pero dio uvas silvestres. Ahora, unos siete siglos después, Jesús está en los atrios del templo en Jerusalén y comienza una historia que todo oyente reconoce de inmediato: "Hubo un hombre, padre de familia, el cual plantó una viña, la cercó de vallado, cavó en ella un lagar, edificó una torre" (Mateo 21:33). El vallado, el lagar y la torre vienen directamente de Isaías 5. La multitud conoce este canto. Pero Jesús añade algo que Isaías nunca dijo. Esta vez el problema no es la viña. Son los labradores.

blocks.en: This parable brings the Old Testament parables of this course to their climax. The vineyard owner of Isaiah 5 finally sends his own son, and the tenants kill him. It is the most openly autobiographical parable Jesus ever told. Within a few days of telling it, it came true.
blocks.es_reference: Esta parábola lleva a su punto culminante las parábolas del Antiguo Testamento de este curso. El dueño de la viña de Isaías 5 finalmente envía a su propio hijo, y los labradores lo matan. Es la parábola más abiertamente autobiográfica que Jesús contó. Pocos días después de contarla, se cumplió.

blocks.en: I. The Setting: A Week of Confrontation
blocks.es_reference: I. El contexto: una semana de confrontación

blocks.en: Matthew places this parable in the last week of Jesus' life. He has entered Jerusalem to the crowd's hosannas (21:1–11), driven the money changers from the temple (21:12–13), and been challenged by the chief priests and elders: "By what authority are You doing these things?" (21:23). Jesus answers with three parables in a row. The parable of the two sons (21:28–32) shows that tax collectors and harlots who repent enter the kingdom ahead of religious leaders who say yes to God but never obey. The parable of the tenants (21:33–46) follows. Then the parable of the wedding banquet (22:1–14) shows invited guests refusing the king's feast. All three answer the question of authority, and all three are aimed at the leaders standing in front of Him.
blocks.es_reference: Mateo coloca esta parábola en la última semana de la vida de Jesús. Ha entrado en Jerusalén entre los hosannas de la multitud (21:1–11), ha echado a los cambistas del templo (21:12–13) y ha sido desafiado por los principales sacerdotes y los ancianos: "¿Con qué autoridad haces estas cosas?" (21:23). Jesús responde con tres parábolas seguidas. La parábola de los dos hijos (21:28–32) muestra que los publicanos y las rameras que se arrepienten entran al reino antes que los líderes religiosos que le dicen sí a Dios pero nunca obedecen. Sigue la parábola de los labradores (21:33–46). Luego la parábola de las bodas (22:1–14) muestra a invitados que rechazan el banquete del rey. Las tres responden a la pregunta de la autoridad, y las tres apuntan a los líderes que están delante de Él.

blocks.en: The leaders understood exactly whom He meant. "Now when the chief priests and Pharisees heard His parables, they perceived that He was speaking of them" (21:45). They wanted to arrest Him on the spot but feared the crowds, who regarded Jesus as a prophet.
blocks.es_reference: Los líderes entendieron exactamente a quién se refería: "Y oyendo sus parábolas los principales sacerdotes y los fariseos, entendieron que hablaba de ellos" (21:45). Querían arrestarlo en ese momento, pero temían a la multitud, que tenía a Jesús por profeta.

blocks.en: II. The Sharecroppers (Matthew 21:33)
blocks.es_reference: II. Los labradores arrendatarios (Mateo 21:33)

blocks.en: The owner planted the vineyard, protected it with a hedge, dug a winepress, built a watchtower, "and he leased it to vinedressers and went into a far country." This was common in Galilee and Judea. Wealthy landowners, often living far away, leased their land to tenant farmers who worked it and paid the rent at harvest, usually as an agreed share of the crop. The owner supplied everything; the tenants supplied the labor and returned a portion of the fruit. Surviving documents from the ancient world show that disputes between absent landlords and tenants were frequent and sometimes violent, so Jesus' hearers knew this situation well.
blocks.es_reference: El dueño plantó la viña, la protegió con un vallado, cavó un lagar, edificó una torre de vigilancia, "y la arrendó a unos labradores, y se fue lejos". Esto era común en Galilea y Judea. Terratenientes ricos, que a menudo vivían lejos, arrendaban su tierra a labradores que la trabajaban y pagaban la renta en la cosecha, normalmente como una parte convenida del fruto. El dueño proveía todo; los labradores ponían el trabajo y devolvían una porción del fruto. Documentos antiguos que se conservan muestran que los pleitos entre dueños ausentes y arrendatarios eran frecuentes y a veces violentos, así que los oyentes de Jesús conocían bien esta situación.

blocks.en: The meaning is not hard to see. God is the owner. The vineyard is Israel and, more broadly, the kingdom of God entrusted to His people. The tenants are the leaders who were responsible for tending it and returning its fruit to God. Every good thing they had came from Him. A sharecropper owns nothing; he manages what belongs to another. "We brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Timothy 6:7). Every Christian, and especially every pastor, is a tenant in God's vineyard, not its owner.
blocks.es_reference: El significado no es difícil de ver. Dios es el dueño. La viña es Israel y, en un sentido más amplio, el reino de Dios confiado a Su pueblo. Los labradores son los líderes responsables de cuidarla y devolver su fruto a Dios. Todo lo bueno que tenían venía de Él. Un arrendatario no es dueño de nada; administra lo que pertenece a otro. "Porque nada hemos traído a este mundo, y sin duda nada podremos sacar" (1 Timoteo 6:7). Todo cristiano, y especialmente todo pastor, es un arrendatario en la viña de Dios, no su dueño.

blocks.en: The owner's journey to "a far country" pictures God's patience. To careless people, God may seem far away, as if He will never come to ask for His fruit. But He is not absent; He is waiting. The long delay is mercy, not indifference.
blocks.es_reference: El viaje del dueño "lejos" representa la paciencia de Dios. A los descuidados, Dios puede parecerles lejano, como si nunca fuera a venir a pedir Su fruto. Pero no está ausente; está esperando. La larga demora es misericordia, no indiferencia.

blocks.en: III. The Servants (Matthew 21:34–36)
blocks.es_reference: III. Los siervos (Mateo 21:34–36)

blocks.en: "Now when vintage-time drew near, he sent his servants to the vinedressers, that they might receive its fruit. And the vinedressers took his servants, beat one, killed one, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they did likewise to them" (21:34–36). The owner was asking only for what was right, what had been agreed from the beginning. The tenants responded with violence.
blocks.es_reference: "Y cuando se acercó el tiempo de los frutos, envió sus siervos a los labradores, para que recibiesen sus frutos. Mas los labradores, tomando a los siervos, a uno golpearon, a otro mataron, y a otro apedrearon. Envió de nuevo otros siervos, más que los primeros; e hicieron con ellos de la misma manera" (21:34–36). El dueño pedía solo lo que era justo, lo que se había convenido desde el principio. Los labradores respondieron con violencia.

blocks.en: The servants are the prophets. The chronicler summed up Israel's history in nearly the same words: "The LORD God of their fathers sent warnings to them by His messengers, rising up early and sending them, because He had compassion on His people... But they mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against His people, till there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). Jeremiah was beaten, imprisoned, and thrown into a cistern (Jeremiah 20:2; 38:6). Jewish and Christian tradition adds that Isaiah was sawn in two, and Hebrews 11:37 may refer to this. John the Baptist, the last of the prophets before Christ, had just been beheaded. Jesus Himself said, "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the one who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her!" (Matthew 23:37).
blocks.es_reference: Los siervos son los profetas. El cronista resumió la historia de Israel casi con las mismas palabras: "Y Jehová el Dios de sus padres envió constantemente palabra a ellos por medio de sus mensajeros, porque él tenía misericordia de su pueblo... Mas ellos hacían escarnio de los mensajeros de Dios, y menospreciaban sus palabras, burlándose de sus profetas, hasta que subió la ira de Jehová contra su pueblo, y no hubo ya remedio" (2 Crónicas 36:15–16). Zacarías hijo de Joiada fue apedreado en el patio del templo (2 Crónicas 24:20–21). Jeremías fue azotado, encarcelado y echado en una cisterna (Jeremías 20:2; 38:6). La tradición judía y cristiana añade que Isaías fue aserrado por la mitad, y Hebreos 11:37 quizás se refiere a esto. Juan el Bautista, el último de los profetas antes de Cristo, acababa de ser decapitado. Jesús mismo dijo: "¡Jerusalén, Jerusalén, que matas a los profetas, y apedreas a los que te son enviados!" (Mateo 23:37).

blocks.en: Notice the owner's astonishing patience. A human landlord would have sent soldiers after the first servant was beaten. This owner sent servant after servant, more each time. That patience is the heart of God. Yet the tenants mistook patience for weakness, as people still do.
blocks.es_reference: Note la asombrosa paciencia del dueño. Un terrateniente humano habría enviado soldados después de que golpearan al primer siervo. Este dueño envió siervo tras siervo, más cada vez. Esa paciencia es el corazón de Dios. Pero los labradores confundieron la paciencia con debilidad, como la gente todavía lo hace.

blocks.en: A Sunday school teacher in Washington once had a mischievous boy in his class who would not listen and kept others from listening. The teacher was discouraged. The boy went west and wasted years in reckless living. Long afterward, after a night of debauchery in Baltimore, he wandered into a cemetery and saw his old teacher's name on a tombstone. Memories of the teacher's words came flooding back. He knelt at the grave and gave his life to Christ, and he later became one of the most beloved pastors in Virginia. The teacher had died believing his work with that boy had failed. God's messengers often do not live to see the fruit of their faithfulness.
blocks.es_reference: Un maestro de escuela dominical en Washington tuvo una vez en su clase a un niño travieso que no escuchaba y no dejaba escuchar a los demás. El maestro se desanimó. El muchacho se fue al oeste y malgastó años en una vida desenfrenada. Mucho después, tras una noche de libertinaje en Baltimore, entró sin rumbo a un cementerio y vio el nombre de su antiguo maestro en una lápida. Los recuerdos de las palabras del maestro volvieron como una inundación. Se arrodilló ante la tumba y entregó su vida a Cristo, y después llegó a ser uno de los pastores más queridos de Virginia. El maestro había muerto creyendo que su obra con aquel muchacho había fracasado. Los mensajeros de Dios muchas veces no viven para ver el fruto de su fidelidad.

blocks.en: IV. The Son (Matthew 21:37–39)
blocks.es_reference: IV. El hijo (Mateo 21:37–39)

blocks.en: "Then last of all he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son'" (21:37). Mark adds that the owner had "one son, his beloved" (Mark 12:6), echoing the voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism: "This is My beloved Son" (Matthew 3:17). Here Jesus tells the leaders, in story form, exactly who He is. He is not one more servant in the line of the prophets. He is the Son and heir.
blocks.es_reference: "Finalmente les envió su hijo, diciendo: Tendrán respeto a mi hijo" (21:37). Marcos añade que el dueño tenía "un hijo suyo, amado" (Marcos 12:6), haciendo eco de la voz del cielo en el bautismo de Jesús: "Este es mi Hijo amado" (Mateo 3:17). Aquí Jesús les dice a los líderes, en forma de historia, exactamente quién es Él. No es un siervo más en la fila de los profetas. Es el Hijo y heredero.

blocks.en: "But when the vinedressers saw the son, they said among themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance.' So they took him and cast him out of the vineyard and killed him" (21:38–39). Their reasoning was as foolish as it was wicked. Some scholars suggest they hoped that, with the heir dead, the property would be treated as ownerless and fall to those who occupied it. They wanted the vineyard without the owner. That is the essence of sin: we want God's gifts without God's rule.
blocks.es_reference: "Mas los labradores, cuando vieron al hijo, dijeron entre sí: Este es el heredero; venid, matémosle, y apoderémonos de su heredad. Y tomándole, le echaron fuera de la viña, y le mataron" (21:38–39). Su razonamiento era tan necio como malvado. Algunos eruditos sugieren que esperaban que, muerto el heredero, la propiedad se considerara sin dueño y pasara a quienes la ocupaban. Querían la viña sin el dueño. Esa es la esencia del pecado: queremos los dones de Dios sin el gobierno de Dios.

blocks.en: The detail that they cast him "out of the vineyard" and then killed him is striking. Within days, Jesus was led outside the walls of Jerusalem and crucified. "Therefore Jesus also, that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, suffered outside the gate" (Hebrews 13:12). The parable is prophecy. Jesus knew exactly what was coming, and He told His killers the story ahead of time, still inviting them to repent.
blocks.es_reference: El detalle de que lo echaron "fuera de la viña" y luego lo mataron es notable. En pocos días, Jesús fue llevado fuera de los muros de Jerusalén y crucificado. "Por lo cual también Jesús, para santificar al pueblo mediante su propia sangre, padeció fuera de la puerta" (Hebreos 13:12). La parábola es profecía. Jesús sabía exactamente lo que venía, y les contó la historia de antemano a quienes lo matarían, invitándolos todavía al arrepentimiento.

blocks.en: V. The Settlement (Matthew 21:40–46)
blocks.es_reference: V. El ajuste de cuentas (Mateo 21:40–46)

blocks.en: Then Jesus asked, "Therefore, when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those vinedressers?" (21:40). This is the method we met with Nathan and David in Unit 5: a juridical parable. The listeners are asked to judge the case, and they pronounce sentence on themselves: "He will destroy those wicked men miserably, and lease his vineyard to other vinedressers who will render to him the fruits in their seasons" (21:41). It is as if we asked, "What should a landlord do with tenants who refuse to pay and kill the rent collector?" Anyone would answer, "Evict them and rent to someone who will pay."
blocks.es_reference: Entonces Jesús preguntó: "Cuando venga, pues, el señor de la viña, ¿qué hará a aquellos labradores?" (21:40). Este es el método que vimos con Natán y David en la Unidad 5: una parábola judicial. Se pide a los oyentes que juzguen el caso, y ellos dictan sentencia contra sí mismos: "A los malos destruirá sin misericordia, y arrendará su viña a otros labradores, que le paguen el fruto a su tiempo" (21:41). Es como si preguntáramos: "¿Qué debe hacer un dueño con inquilinos que se niegan a pagar y matan al cobrador?" Cualquiera respondería: "Desalojarlos y rentar a alguien que pague."

blocks.en: Jesus then quoted Psalm 118:22–23: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. This was the LORD's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes" (21:42). The image changes from farming to building, but the point continues. The leaders, the "builders," were rejecting the very stone God had chosen to hold the whole building together. Many interpreters note a wordplay in Hebrew between ben, "son," and eben, "stone." The rejected Son is the chosen Stone. The rejection would not defeat God's plan; it would fulfill it through the resurrection.
blocks.es_reference: Luego Jesús citó el Salmo 118:22–23: "La piedra que desecharon los edificadores, ha venido a ser cabeza del ángulo. El Señor ha hecho esto, y es cosa maravillosa a nuestros ojos" (21:42). La imagen cambia de la agricultura a la construcción, pero el punto continúa. Los líderes, los "edificadores", rechazaban la misma piedra que Dios había escogido para sostener todo el edificio. Muchos intérpretes notan un juego de palabras en hebreo entre ben, "hijo", y eben, "piedra". El Hijo rechazado es la Piedra escogida. El rechazo no frustraría el plan de Dios; lo cumpliría por medio de la resurrección.

blocks.en: "Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation bearing the fruits of it" (21:43). Christians have understood this verse in different ways, and it must be handled with care. Some have read it as God rejecting the Jewish people as a whole and replacing them with the church. Most careful interpreters today point out that the parable is aimed at the leaders, who "perceived that He was speaking of them" (21:45); that the first "nation bearing the fruits" was the community of Jesus' followers, all of them Jews at first, which soon welcomed Gentiles; and that Paul insists "God has not cast away His people whom He foreknew" (Romans 11:2). The warning is not ethnic pride on our part. It is a warning to every steward, Jewish or Gentile, who receives God's vineyard and refuses to give Him its fruit.
blocks.es_reference: "Por tanto os digo, que el reino de Dios será quitado de vosotros, y será dado a gente que produzca los frutos de él" (21:43). Los cristianos han entendido este versículo de maneras diferentes, y debe tratarse con cuidado. Algunos lo han leído como si Dios rechazara al pueblo judío en su conjunto y lo reemplazara con la iglesia. La mayoría de los intérpretes cuidadosos hoy señalan que la parábola va dirigida a los líderes, que "entendieron que hablaba de ellos" (21:45); que la primera "gente que produzca los frutos" fue la comunidad de los seguidores de Jesús, todos judíos al principio, que pronto recibió a los gentiles; y que Pablo insiste en que "no ha desechado Dios a su pueblo, al cual desde antes conoció" (Romanos 11:2). La advertencia no es motivo de orgullo étnico para nosotros. Es una advertencia para todo mayordomo, judío o gentil, que recibe la viña de Dios y se niega a darle su fruto.

blocks.en: The settlement came about forty years later, when Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70. As we saw in Unit 2, God's patience is great but not endless. Yet even in judgment the parable points to grace. The Son whom the builders rejected became the cornerstone of a new temple made of living stones (1 Peter 2:4–7), where anyone who comes to Him is welcome.
blocks.es_reference: El ajuste de cuentas llegó unos cuarenta años después, cuando los ejércitos romanos destruyeron Jerusalén y su templo en el año 70 d. C. Como vimos en la Unidad 2, la paciencia de Dios es grande pero no interminable. Sin embargo, aun en el juicio la parábola apunta a la gracia. El Hijo que rechazaron los edificadores llegó a ser la piedra angular de un templo nuevo hecho de piedras vivas (1 Pedro 2:4–7), donde todo el que viene a Él es bienvenido.

blocks.en: VI. What Fruit Does God Expect?
blocks.es_reference: VI. ¿Qué fruto espera Dios?

blocks.en: The whole parable turns on fruit. The owner sent his servants "that they might receive its fruit" (21:34), and Jesus said the kingdom would be given "to a nation bearing the fruits of it" (21:43). What fruit does God look for? Scripture answers in several ways, and together they give a full picture.
blocks.es_reference: Toda la parábola gira en torno al fruto. El dueño envió a sus siervos "para que recibiesen sus frutos" (21:34), y Jesús dijo que el reino sería dado "a gente que produzca los frutos de él" (21:43). ¿Qué fruto busca Dios? La Escritura responde de varias maneras, y juntas dan un cuadro completo.

blocks.en: First, fruit is character: "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:22–23). Second, fruit is righteous conduct, the justice and mercy Isaiah looked for in the vineyard (Isaiah 5:7) and that Paul prayed would fill the believers, "being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are by Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:11). Third, fruit is good works done for others, "being fruitful in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God" (Colossians 1:10). Fourth, fruit includes people brought to God; Paul longed to visit Rome "that I might have some fruit among you also" (Romans 1:13). And fifth, fruit is praise: "the fruit of our lips, giving thanks to His name" (Hebrews 13:15).
blocks.es_reference: Primero, el fruto es carácter: "el fruto del Espíritu es amor, gozo, paz, paciencia, benignidad, bondad, fe, mansedumbre, templanza" (Gálatas 5:22–23). Segundo, el fruto es conducta justa, la justicia y la misericordia que Isaías buscaba en la viña (Isaías 5:7) y que Pablo pidió que llenaran a los creyentes, "llenos de frutos de justicia que son por medio de Jesucristo" (Filipenses 1:11). Tercero, el fruto son buenas obras hechas por otros, "llevando fruto en toda buena obra, y creciendo en el conocimiento de Dios" (Colosenses 1:10). Cuarto, el fruto incluye personas traídas a Dios; Pablo anhelaba visitar Roma "para tener también entre vosotros algún fruto" (Romanos 1:13). Y quinto, el fruto es alabanza: "fruto de labios que confiesan su nombre" (Hebreos 13:15).

blocks.en: Notice that none of this fruit is produced by our own strength. Jesus said, "He who abides in Me, and I in him, bears much fruit; for without Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). The tenants failed not because the vineyard was poor but because they wanted to keep for themselves what belonged to the owner. The religious leaders had temples, sacrifices, schools, and traditions, but they would not give God what He was actually seeking: repentant hearts, lives of justice and mercy, and faith in the Son He sent. The same danger faces every church. Activity is not the same as fruit. God is not impressed by the size of the vineyard but by what it yields for Him.
blocks.es_reference: Note que nada de este fruto se produce con nuestras propias fuerzas. Jesús dijo: "El que permanece en mí, y yo en él, éste lleva mucho fruto; porque separados de mí nada podéis hacer" (Juan 15:5). Los labradores no fallaron porque la viña fuera pobre, sino porque quisieron quedarse con lo que pertenecía al dueño. Los líderes religiosos tenían templo, sacrificios, escuelas y tradiciones, pero no querían darle a Dios lo que Él realmente buscaba: corazones arrepentidos, vidas de justicia y misericordia, y fe en el Hijo que Él envió. El mismo peligro enfrenta toda iglesia. La actividad no es lo mismo que el fruto. A Dios no le impresiona el tamaño de la viña, sino lo que produce para Él.

blocks.en: VII. The Mirror for Today
blocks.es_reference: VII. El espejo para hoy

blocks.en: Jesus' parables are mirrors, and this one is held up before every church and every pastor. We are tenants, not owners. God has entrusted us with His word, His people, His gifts, and His mission. He looks for fruit: faithful teaching, changed lives, justice and mercy, and the good news carried to those who have not heard. Leaders are especially warned. It is possible to be busy in the vineyard and still treat it as our own, protecting our positions and resenting anyone God sends to call us back to Him.
blocks.es_reference: Las parábolas de Jesús son espejos, y esta se pone delante de toda iglesia y todo pastor. Somos arrendatarios, no dueños. Dios nos ha confiado Su palabra, Su pueblo, Sus dones y Su misión. Busca fruto: enseñanza fiel, vidas transformadas, justicia y misericordia, y las buenas nuevas llevadas a quienes no las han oído. Los líderes son advertidos especialmente. Es posible estar ocupados en la viña y aun así tratarla como nuestra, protegiendo nuestras posiciones y resintiendo a cualquiera que Dios envíe para llamarnos de vuelta a Él.

blocks.en: The parable also calls for a personal response to the Son. The leaders knew the story was about them, and still they sought to arrest Him. Knowing the truth is not enough. The question the parable leaves with each reader is simple: when the Owner sends His Son, will we receive Him or reject Him?
blocks.es_reference: La parábola también llama a una respuesta personal ante el Hijo. Los líderes sabían que la historia hablaba de ellos, y aun así buscaron arrestarlo. Conocer la verdad no basta. La pregunta que la parábola deja a cada lector es sencilla: cuando el Dueño envía a Su Hijo, ¿lo recibiremos o lo rechazaremos?

blocks.en: VIII. Preaching the Tenants
blocks.es_reference: VIII. Cómo predicar a los labradores

blocks.en: A clear outline follows the parable's own movement with four words: the Sharecroppers, entrusted with God's vineyard; the Servants, God's patient messengers rejected again and again; the Son, the final and greatest messenger, cast out and killed; and the Settlement, when the Owner comes to judge. Link the sermon to Isaiah 5 so hearers feel the weight of seven centuries of God's patience. Handle verse 43 carefully, avoiding any hint of contempt for the Jewish people. End at the cornerstone: the rejected Son is now the risen Lord, and every tenant can still come to Him.
blocks.es_reference: Un bosquejo claro sigue el propio movimiento de la parábola con cuatro palabras: los arrendatarios, a quienes se confió la viña de Dios; los siervos, los mensajeros pacientes de Dios rechazados una y otra vez; el Hijo, el último y mayor mensajero, echado fuera y muerto; y el ajuste de cuentas, cuando el Dueño viene a juzgar. Relacione el sermón con Isaías 5 para que los oyentes sientan el peso de siete siglos de paciencia de Dios. Trate el versículo 43 con cuidado, evitando cualquier indicio de desprecio hacia el pueblo judío. Termine en la piedra angular: el Hijo rechazado es ahora el Señor resucitado, y todo arrendatario todavía puede venir a Él.

blocks.en: Closing
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: The Owner of the vineyard gave everything: the land, the wall, the tower, the winepress. He sent servant after servant, and finally His beloved Son. The tenants cast Him out and killed Him, and it seemed that they had won. But the stone the builders rejected became the chief cornerstone. The same Son who was killed outside the gate rose again, and He still asks for the fruit of the vineyard. May we be tenants who gladly give the Owner what is His, and who welcome His Son.
blocks.es_reference: El Dueño de la viña lo dio todo: la tierra, el vallado, la torre, el lagar. Envió siervo tras siervo, y finalmente a Su Hijo amado. Los labradores lo echaron fuera y lo mataron, y pareció que habían ganado. Pero la piedra que desecharon los edificadores llegó a ser cabeza del ángulo. El mismo Hijo que fue muerto fuera de la puerta resucitó, y todavía pide el fruto de la viña. Que seamos arrendatarios que con gusto dan al Dueño lo que es Suyo, y que reciben a Su Hijo.

— Dr. Wayne Cook
Chapala Theological Seminary

mc.stem: The details of the hedge, winepress, and tower in Matthew 21:33 come from:
mc.why: Every listener recognized Isaiah's song, but Jesus shifted the problem from the vineyard to the tenants.

mc.stem: Jesus told this parable during:
options: The last week of His life, in the temple courts
His childhood visit to the temple
mc.why: It answered the leaders' challenge about His authority (Matthew 21:23).

mc.stem: Which three parables does Matthew place together in response to the question of authority?
options: The sower, the tares, and the mustard seed
The two sons, the tenants, and the wedding banquet
The lost sheep, coin, and son
The talents, virgins, and sheep and goats
mc.why: All three were aimed at the leaders standing in front of Him.

mc.stem: In the ancient tenant-farming system, the tenants paid:
options: A fixed tax to Rome only
An agreed share of the crop at harvest
mc.why: The owner supplied everything; the tenants supplied labor and returned a share.

mc.stem: In the parable, the tenants represent:
options: The leaders responsible for tending God's vineyard
mc.why: The chief priests and Pharisees perceived that He was speaking of them (21:45).

mc.stem: The owner's journey to "a far country" pictures:
options: God's patience, waiting rather than being absent
mc.why: The long delay is mercy, not indifference.

mc.stem: The servants whom the owner sent represent:
mc.why: 2 Chronicles 36:15–16 summarizes Israel's rejection of God's messengers.

mc.stem: Which prophet does Scripture record was stoned in the temple court?
mc.why: See 2 Chronicles 24:20–21; tradition adds that Isaiah was sawn in two.

mc.stem: The owner's repeated sending of servants shows:
options: That he did not care about the fruit
That he was afraid of the tenants
That he had too many servants
Astonishing patience, which the tenants mistook for weakness
mc.why: A human landlord would have sent soldiers after the first servant was beaten.

mc.stem: The Sunday school teacher who died thinking he had failed illustrates that:
options: God's messengers often do not live to see the fruit of their faithfulness
mc.why: The boy was converted at his teacher's grave and became a beloved pastor.

mc.stem: Mark's phrase "one son, his beloved" echoes:
options: The voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism
mc.why: "This is My beloved Son" (Matthew 3:17): Jesus is not one more servant but the Son and heir.

mc.stem: According to this unit, the tenants' plan to kill the heir reveals the essence of sin, which is:
options: Wanting God's gifts without God's rule
mc.why: They wanted the vineyard without the owner.

mc.stem: The son being cast "out of the vineyard" before he was killed corresponds to:
options: Jesus suffering outside the gate of Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:12)
mc.why: The parable is prophecy; Jesus told His killers the story ahead of time.

mc.stem: Jesus' question "What will he do to those vinedressers?" makes this a:
options: Juridical parable, in which the hearers sentence themselves
mc.why: The same method Nathan used with David in Unit 5.

mc.stem: Jesus quoted Psalm 118:22, "The stone which the builders rejected," to show that:
options: The rejected Son would become the chosen cornerstone
mc.why: Many note the Hebrew wordplay between ben (son) and eben (stone).

mc.stem: How does this unit recommend understanding Matthew 21:43, "the kingdom will be taken from you"?
options: As proof God has permanently rejected all Jews
As aimed at the leaders, not a rejection of the Jewish people, who remain loved (Romans 11:2)
mc.why: The first fruitful "nation" was Jesus' Jewish followers, soon joined by Gentiles.

mc.stem: The "settlement" Jesus predicted came when:
options: Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70
mc.why: About forty years after Jesus told the parable.

mc.stem: According to this unit, how does the parable serve as a mirror for pastors today?
options: We are tenants, not owners, and must give God the fruit of His vineyard
mc.why: It is possible to be busy in the vineyard and still treat it as our own.

mc.stem: The four-word preaching outline in this unit is:
mc.why: It follows the parable's own movement from Wayne Cook's sermon outline.

mc.stem: The question the parable leaves with each reader is:
options: When the Owner sends His Son, will we receive Him or reject Him?
How much rent should tenants pay?
mc.why: Knowing the truth is not enough; the leaders knew and still rejected Him.

sa.prompt: Explain how the parable of the tenants connects to Isaiah 5 and what new element Jesus adds.
sa.model: Jesus opens with the hedge, winepress, and tower of Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard, where God looked for good grapes and found wild grapes. Every hearer recognized it. But Jesus adds tenants, so the problem is no longer the vineyard's fruit but the leaders entrusted with it, and He adds the owner's son, whom they kill. It brings the Old Testament parables of the course to their climax.

sa.prompt: Describe the setting of the parable in Matthew 21 and its companion parables.
sa.model: In the last week of His life, after the triumphal entry and cleansing the temple, Jesus was challenged by the chief priests and elders about His authority. He answered with three parables: the two sons, the tenants, and the wedding banquet, all aimed at the leaders. The chief priests and Pharisees perceived that He was speaking of them and wanted to arrest Him, but they feared the crowds.

sa.prompt: Explain the ancient tenant-farming system and what the owner, vineyard, and tenants represent.
sa.model: Wealthy landowners, often living far away, leased their land to tenants who worked it and paid an agreed share of the crop at harvest; disputes were common. God is the owner, the vineyard is Israel and the kingdom entrusted to His people, and the tenants are the leaders responsible to return its fruit. A tenant owns nothing but manages what belongs to another, as every Christian and pastor does in God's vineyard.

sa.prompt: Explain who the servants represent, with biblical examples, and what the owner's patience teaches.
sa.model: The servants are the prophets. 2 Chronicles 36 says God sent His messengers because He had compassion, but they mocked and scoffed at them. Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court, Jeremiah was beaten and thrown in a cistern, tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two, and John the Baptist was beheaded. The owner sent servant after servant, showing astonishing patience, which the tenants mistook for weakness.

sa.prompt: Explain the meaning of the son in the parable and how the details point to Jesus' death.
sa.model: The owner sent his son, whom Mark calls his beloved, echoing the voice at Jesus' baptism; Jesus is not another servant but the Son and heir. The tenants reasoned that by killing the heir they could seize the inheritance, wanting the vineyard without the owner, the essence of sin: God's gifts without God's rule. They cast him out of the vineyard and killed him, as Jesus suffered outside the gate of Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:12).

sa.prompt: Explain how the settlement in Matthew 21:40–42 works as a juridical parable and the meaning of the rejected stone.
sa.model: Jesus asked what the owner would do, and the hearers answered that he would destroy those wicked men and lease the vineyard to others, pronouncing sentence on themselves, the method Nathan used with David. Jesus then quoted Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected became the chief cornerstone. The leaders rejected the stone God chose; many note the Hebrew wordplay of ben, son, and eben, stone. The rejected Son became the cornerstone through the resurrection.

sa.prompt: Explain how to interpret Matthew 21:43 carefully, presenting the views fairly.
sa.model: Some have read "the kingdom will be taken from you" as God rejecting the Jewish people and replacing them with the church. Most careful interpreters note the parable targets the leaders, who knew He spoke of them; the first fruitful people were Jesus' Jewish followers, soon joined by Gentiles; and Paul insists God has not cast away His people (Romans 11:2). The warning applies to every steward, Jewish or Gentile, who withholds fruit.

sa.prompt: Explain how the parable was fulfilled historically and how it still points to grace.
sa.model: About forty years later, in AD 70, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple; as Unit 2 taught, God's patience is great but not endless. Yet the parable still points to grace: the Son whom the builders rejected became the cornerstone of a new temple of living stones (1 Peter 2:4–7), where anyone who comes to Him is welcome.

sa.prompt: Explain how the parable serves as a mirror for churches and pastors today.
sa.model: We are tenants, not owners. God has entrusted us with His word, people, gifts, and mission, and He looks for fruit: faithful teaching, changed lives, justice and mercy, and the gospel carried to others. Leaders are especially warned, because it is possible to be busy in the vineyard and still treat it as ours, protecting our positions. The parable also asks each person whether he will receive or reject the Son.

sa.prompt: Give the four-word outline for preaching the tenants and the cautions for the sermon.
sa.model: The outline follows the parable: the Sharecroppers entrusted with the vineyard, the Servants rejected again and again, the Son cast out and killed, and the Settlement when the Owner comes to judge. Link it to Isaiah 5 so hearers feel seven centuries of God's patience. Handle verse 43 carefully, avoiding any contempt for the Jewish people, and end at the cornerstone: the rejected Son is the risen Lord, and anyone can still come to Him.
